title: China: Baijiu Aroma Types & Huangjiu (GB National Standards)
attribution: China classifies its two great indigenous drink families by binding GB national standards. Baijiu — the world's most-consumed spirit by volume — is defined by GB/T 15109 (terminology) and a family of aroma-type standards (xiangxing) that key the spirit to its fermentation vessel, grain and qū (starter). Huangjiu, the ancient rice/millet wine, is defined by GB/T 13662 and, for Shaoxing, a protected geographical-indication standard. Figures are typical commercial values; the aroma-type definitions are the legally meaningful classification. Compiled from the GB standards and industry sources.

styles.name: Nongxiang / Strong Aroma (浓香型)
styles.impression: The dominant baijiu style by volume: rich, sweet-savoury, pineapple-and-overripe-fruit esters over a mellow grain base.
styles.comments: The mud-pit fermentation is continuous and the oldest pits are prized — some in use for centuries. Ethyl hexanoate is the marker compound. Luzhou Laojiao and Wuliangye are the archetypes.
styles.ingredients: Sorghum (and often a five-grain blend), fermented in aged mud pits (jiaochi) whose microbial community is the key to the ethyl caproate that defines the aroma. Medium-temperature Daqu wheat starter.

styles.name: Jiangxiang / Sauce Aroma (酱香型)
styles.impression: The most complex and expensive style: deep soy-sauce, umami, dried mushroom and toasted notes from an elaborate year-long process.
styles.comments: Kweichow Moutai is the national archetype and diplomatic gift. The high-temperature qū and repeated fermentation build hundreds of pyrazine and furan compounds.
styles.ingredients: Sorghum with high-temperature Daqu, fermented in stone pits, distilled across seven-to-eight rounds over a full year with multiple firings, then aged for years and blended.

styles.name: Qingxiang / Light Aroma (清香型)
styles.impression: Clean, dry, delicate and floral — the most restrained baijiu, with a crisp grain purity.
styles.comments: The stone/ceramic vessel is what keeps it 'clean' — no mud microflora. Ethyl acetate and ethyl lactate dominate over the heavier caproate esters.
styles.ingredients: Sorghum fermented in stone or ceramic jars (not mud), keeping the ferment clean; low-temperature Daqu. Fen-jiu is the classic.

styles.name: Mixiang / Rice Aroma (米香型)
styles.impression: Soft, mild, honeyed and slightly floral — distilled from rice rather than sorghum, the gentlest of the classic types.
styles.comments: Beta-phenylethanol gives a rose-honey top note. Sanhua Jiu of Guilin is the benchmark.
styles.ingredients: Rice, fermented with small Xiaoqu rice-cake starter, then distilled. Southern China, especially Guilin.

styles.name: Other Aroma Types (其他香型)
styles.impression: The GB framework recognises further types — phoenix (fengxiang), sesame (zhimaxiang), mixed/jian, special, laobaigan, chi, and more — each tied to a region and technique.
styles.comments: Twelve aroma types are formally recognised. Fengxiang (Xifeng, Shaanxi) ages in wicker baskets lined with pig-blood paper; zhimaxiang shows a roasted-sesame note.

styles.name: Shaoxing Huangjiu (绍兴黄酒, GI)
styles.impression: The benchmark rice wine: amber, warming, savoury-sweet with a nutty, umami depth. Drunk warmed, and the backbone of Chinese cooking wine.
styles.comments: A protected GI. Sub-types by residual sugar: Yuanhong (dry), Jiafan (semi-dry), Shanniang (semi-sweet), Xiangxue (sweet). Nü'er Hong ('daughter red') was buried at a daughter's birth and unearthed for her wedding.
styles.ingredients: Glutinous rice and wheat qū, fermented with the soft water of Jian Lake, aged in earthenware. Multiple parallel fermentation like sake, but with a mixed-mould wheat starter rather than koji.

styles.name: Huangjiu by Sweetness Class
styles.impression: GB/T 13662 classes huangjiu by residual sugar: dry (≤15 g/L), semi-dry (15.1–40), semi-sweet (40.1–100) and sweet (>100 g/L).
styles.comments: Distinct from sake in starter (mixed-culture wheat qū vs Aspergillus oryzae koji) and in being typically unfiltered-then-clarified and aged oxidatively.
styles.ingredients: Rice (glutinous, japonica or black), or millet in the north; wheat or rice qū.
